title: The Penny Black
hook: The world's first stamp is why British stamps still carry no country name.
peek: In 1840 Britain issued the Penny Black, the first adhesive postage stamp. Because it came first, Britain never needed to print its name on stamps, and to this day a small portrait of the monarch is enough to show where a British stamp comes from.
lede: Before 1840, British letters were usually paid for by the person receiving them, at prices that rose with distance. Rowland Hill argued for a cheap flat rate, paid in advance by the sender. The result was the Penny Black, issued on 1 May 1840 and valid from 6 May. It showed a young Queen Victoria and no country name at all.

bullets.text: Britain was the only country using stamps, so no name was needed. When international rules later asked stamps to name their country, Britain kept an exception as the first issuer. A profile of the monarch's head still does that job.

Hill's Uniform Penny Post let a letter of up to half an ounce travel anywhere in Britain for one penny. Letter writing boomed, and within a few years other countries copied both the flat rate and the sticky stamp.
Each stamp had two letters in its bottom corners, showing its position on the printing sheet. No two stamps on a sheet shared the same pair, which made forgery harder.

bullets.opening: The switch to the Penny Red
bullets.text: The Penny Black lasted less than a year. Red cancellation marks were hard to see on black and could be cleaned off for reuse, so in 1841 the stamp turned red and the marks turned black.
